summary: The note traces the early history of the Forbidden City, beginning with the Mongol Yuan Dynasty's Imperial city on the site and the Ming Dynasty's subsequent changes. After the Yuan collapsed, the Hongwu Emperor moved the capital to Nanjing and ordered the Yuan palaces razed in 1369. The Yongle Emperor, formerly Prince of Yan, usurped the throne in 1402, made Beijing a secondary capital, and began building the Forbidden City in 1406, with its plan reviewed by the Ministry of Work and chief architects including Cai Xin and Nguyen An.
one_line: Early history of the Forbidden City, from the Yuan palaces through the Ming Dynasty's Yongle Emperor and the start of construction in 1406.
key_facts: The site of the Forbidden City was situated on the Imperial city during the Mongol Yuan Dynasty.
After the collapse of the Yuan Dynasty, the Hongwu Emperor of the Ming Dynasty moved the capital from Beijing in the north to Nanjing in the south.
In 1369, the Hongwu Emperor ordered that the Yuan palaces be razed.
The Hongwu Emperor's son Zhu Di was created Prince of Yan with his seat in Beijing.
In 1402, Zhu Di usurped the throne and became the Yongle Emperor.
The Yongle Emperor made Beijing a secondary capital of the Ming empire.
Construction began in 1406 of what would become the Forbidden City.
The Forbidden City's plan was designed by many architects and designers.
The plan of the Forbidden City was examined by the Emperor's Ministry of Work.
Cai Xin is named among the chief architects and engineers of the Forbidden City.
Nguyen An, a Vietnamese eunuch, is named among the chief architects and engineers of the Forbidden City.
Kuai Xiang and Lu Xiang are named among the chief architects and engineers of the Forbidden City.
